causal_claim.content: Radioactive decay of a parent-atom-containing defect destroys or transforms the parent-related color center, so its photoluminescence (PL) decays in time according to the radioactive decay law; conversely, defects associated with the daughter element can show PL growth with the same decay law. Depending on whether the monitored defect contains the parent or daughter element, the PL signal decreases or increases accordingly, and the implanted isotope half-life sets the timescale of this PL evolution.
evidence_spans: As a result, any color center involving the parent atom is either destroyed or transformed upon decay, causing the 3 corresponding PL signal to decay in time following the radioactive decay law.
The reverse also holds: PL features associated with the daughter element may grow in time according to the same decay law.

Depending on whether the monitored defect contains the parent or the daughter element of the decay chain, the corresponding PL signal decreases or increases with time according to the radioactive decay law.
Consequently, the half-life of the implanted isotope sets the timescale of the observed PL signal evolution.

causal_claim.content: Monitoring the temporal evolution of PL allows direct association of spectral features with the implanted chemical element: features whose intensity changes in correlation with radioactive decay can be assigned to the radioactive isotope or its daughter, whereas features with no time dependence are unrelated. In the reported measurements, the PL evolution directly tracked radioactive decay, confirming the element-specific capability of rPL and the implemented setup; specifically, the emission band above 600 nm and a half-life match confirmed a germanium-related origin and demonstrated element-specific PL assignment by rPL.
evidence_spans: By monitoring the temporal evolution of the PL spectrum, spectral features that correlate with the radioactive decay can be directly associated with the im- planted element.
Furthermore, features that exhibit no time dependence are not related to the radioactive isotope.

We show that the temporal evolution of the PL signal directly correlates with the radioactive decay, confirming the element-specific capability of the rPL approach, as well as the effective performance of the implemented setup.

We therefore conclude that the emission band above 600 nm is associated with a germanium-related defect, thereby demonstrating the capability of rPL to link spectral features to the corresponding chemical element.

causal_claim.content: Using Bayesian inference accommodates the stable-limit case by incorporating prior information, yielding robust parameter estimates with rigorous uncertainty intervals; in particular, parameterizing the decay with I0 and f improves posterior geometry, makes sampling easier, and gives smooth behavior in the no-decay limit expected for time-constant regions.

The decay was parametrized in terms of I0 and f instead of the amplitude of the decay and a background constant as it results in a posterior density geometry that is easier to sample from. causal_claim.content: At the GeV− peak, an extremely narrow prior shifts the inferred half-life slightly toward the prior value, but once the prior uncertainty exceeds about 30 min the inferred half-life becomes stable and insensitive to further widening; this indicates that the data overwhelm the prior and the extracted half-life is a robust experimentally determined property.
evidence_spans: At the GeV−peak (602.8 nm), if we force an extremely restrictive, narrow prior (σ = 6 or 12 minutes), the final calculated half-life shifts slightly toward the prior choice (around 5 %).
However, as soon as the prior uncertainty is allowed to expand past σ = 30 min, the final calculated half-life locks onto a stable value and becomes insensitive to how much wider we make the prior.

This demon- strates that our experimental data is highly informative. The data completely overwhelms the prior, proving that the extracted half-life is a robust physical property determined by the experiment itself.
